title: Discovery of the Electron — Cathode Rays
topicTitle: Discovery Of Electron And Its Properties
notes: The discovery of the electron through cathode-ray experiments — the first subatomic particle, and the starting point of every atomic model. (It sits in this unit as the experimental foundation of electronic structure.)

• A gas at low pressure (≈10⁻² atm) in a discharge tube with ≈10 000 V across the electrodes emits rays from the cathode that travel in straight lines (shadow of the Maltese cross), carry momentum (paddle-wheel rotation) and heat the target.
• **Electric field:** the rays bend toward the positive plate → negatively charged.
• **Magnetic field:** they bend in the direction expected for negative charges.
• The deflection is independent of the gas and cathode material → the particle is a universal constituent of all matter.

Crossed E and B fields (velocity selector): undeflected when Eq = Bqv → v = E/B. Then switching off B gives the deflection, yielding e/m = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹ — about 1837 times larger than the hydrogen ion's e/m. Since the charge is later shown to be the same unit charge, the particle must be ≈1837 times lighter than hydrogen: a new particle, the electron.

Balancing the electric force against the weight of a charged oil drop gave the charge of a single electron: e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (quantised — all drops carry integer multiples of e). Combined with e/m, the electron mass is m = 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg (0.000549 u).
### Why this matters for the atomic models

Once atoms contain light negative electrons, something positive must balance them — the direct motivation for Thomson's plum-pudding model and then Rutherford's nucleus. The electron also completes the electronic-structure story: its arrangement in orbitals is what this unit's quantum numbers describe.
confusion: ❌ Cathode rays are electromagnetic waves. ✅ They are streams of charged particles — waves are not deflected by E/B fields.
❌ The cathode-ray properties depend on the gas used. ✅ They are independent of gas and electrode material, which is why the particle is universal.
❌ Millikan measured e/m. ✅ He measured e alone; Thomson had already measured e/m.

summary: Cathode rays revealed the first subatomic particle. In a discharge tube containing a gas at ≈10⁻² atm with about 10 000 V across the electrodes, rays leave the cathode and travel in straight lines (casting the shadow of a Maltese cross), carry momentum (turning a paddle wheel) and heat the target. They bend towards the positive plate in an electric field and in the direction expected for negative charges in a magnetic field, so they are streams of particles, not waves. Crucially the deflection is the same whatever gas and cathode material are used, so the particle is universal. Thomson (1897) used crossed fields as a velocity selector, Eq = Bqv giving v = E/B, and measured e/m = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹, about 1837 times the hydrogen ion's ratio; Millikan's oil-drop experiment (1909) then gave e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and hence mₑ = 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
importantConcepts: Cathode-ray properties: straight-line travel, momentum (paddle wheel), heating effect, deflection by E and B fields
Negative charge deduced from bending towards the positive plate; not electromagnetic radiation
Independence of gas and cathode material, so the electron is a universal constituent of all matter
Thomson's velocity selector Eq = Bqv gives v = E/B, and e/m = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹
Millikan's oil-drop experiment (1909) measured e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, giving mₑ = 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg
importantStatements: Cathode rays are streams of charged particles; electromagnetic waves are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields.
The e/m of cathode rays is independent of the gas and electrode material used.
Thomson measured e/m; Millikan measured the charge e alone — the two milestones are distinct.
The electron is about 1837 times lighter than a hydrogen atom and is the lightest charged particle known.
Since atoms are neutral, the discovery of the electron forced the existence of positive charge in the atom.

keyPoints: Three milestones: cathode rays (nature of the beam), e/m (Thomson, 1897), e (Millikan, 1909).
Velocity selector condition: undeflected when Eq = Bqv, so v = E/B.
Thomson received the 1906 Nobel Prize and Millikan the 1923 Nobel Prize.
The electron's discovery created the need for positive charge — the direct route to Thomson's model and then the nucleus.
specialNotes: The rays travel in straight lines yet are deflected by fields — the combination that identifies them as particles.
Cathode rays are the same regardless of the residual gas, which is the strongest evidence for universality.
Millikan's drops all carried whole-number multiples of e, showing charge is quantised.
examShortTricks: Property → conclusion pairs score best: straight lines and shadow = particles with mass; bending = negative charge.
For velocity problems use v = E/B directly — no other formula is needed.
Link the electron to the 'atom must be neutral' argument; that link is worth a mark every time.
examNotes: Properties with conclusions plus the e/m measurement is a standard 4–5 mark question.
A 2-mark numerical on the undeflected speed (v = E/B) is common.
One-mark items ask who discovered the electron or the value of e/m.
